q: Management accounting is said to be selective in nature because it:

options.A: Records only those transactions which are selected by the statutory auditor
options.B: Takes from the financial and cost data only such information as is relevant and useful for a managerial purpose, instead of presenting the whole data
options.C: Is applied only to a few selected departments of the enterprise
options.D: Selects only the profitable products for reporting to management

e: Management accounting is selective because it picks from financial and cost data only the information relevant and useful for a specific managerial purpose, not the whole data.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Management accounting looks ahead and makes extensive use of estimates, forecasts and budgets, and is not confined to facts already recorded.
2. A management accounting report can be used by management only if it is drawn in a form prescribed by statute.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is correct: it is forward-looking and uses estimates, forecasts and budgets. Statement 2 is wrong as no statute prescribes the form of its reports, so only 1 holds.

q: As a discipline, management accounting draws most of its underlying recorded data from:

options.A: Market surveys conducted among customers
options.B: Physical inspection of stocks and assets alone
options.C: The financial accounting and cost accounting records, which it rearranges, analyses and interprets for management
options.D: Notifications and circulars issued by the Government

e: Its recorded base comes from financial and cost accounting records, which it rearranges, analyses and interprets for management use.

q: A recognised limitation of management accounting is that it:

options.A: Cannot be applied in a large organisation
options.B: Involves no use of cost data at all
options.C: Makes the preparation of budgets unnecessary
options.D: Is a comparatively costly system needing trained staff, so a small concern may find its installation and running uneconomical

e: It is a costly system needing trained staff and elaborate records, so installation and running costs may be uneconomical for a small concern.

q: Management accounting by itself does not guarantee good results mainly because it:

options.A: Only supplies information, analyses and alternatives; the final judgement, the decision and the action on it remain with management
options.B: Is concerned only with the cash transactions of the enterprise
options.C: Ignores the future and deals only with the past
options.D: Replaces the financial accounts of the enterprise

e: It only supplies information, analyses and alternatives; judgement, decision and action remain with management, so good results are not guaranteed by the system alone.

q: A management accountant collects the functional budgets prepared by the several departments, removes inconsistencies among them and consolidates them into a master budget for approval. In doing so, he is performing the function of:

options.A: Statutory audit of the budgets
options.B: Custody of the cash and funds of the enterprise
options.C: Assessment of the tax liability of the enterprise
options.D: Co-ordination of departmental plans through the budgetary system

e: Consolidating departmental budgets, removing inconsistencies and forming the master budget is co-ordination of departmental plans through the budgetary system.

q: An enterprise asks its management accountant to devise the procedure for collecting cost data and to settle the form, contents and periodicity of the reports to be sent to each department. This work forms part of his function of:

options.A: Fixing the selling prices of the products
options.B: Designing and installing a suitable accounting and reporting system for the enterprise
options.C: Negotiating wage settlements with the workers
options.D: Certifying the annual accounts for the shareholders

e: Devising cost-data collection procedure and the form, contents and periodicity of departmental reports is designing and installing the accounting and reporting system.

q: Financial accounting reports the result of the enterprise as a whole for a period. Management accounting, in contrast, commonly reports:

options.A: Also only for the enterprise as a whole
options.B: Only for the use of the tax authorities
options.C: By product, department, territory or activity, that is, by the segment about which a decision is to be taken
options.D: Only once, at the end of the financial year

e: Unlike whole-enterprise financial reporting, management accounting reports by segment - product, department, territory or activity - about which a decision is to be taken.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Financial accounting lays stress on precision and verifiability of the facts recorded.
2. Management accounting lays stress on relevance and promptness of information, and may use reasonable estimates where waiting for exact figures would make the information useless for the decision.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

e: Both hold: financial accounting stresses precision and verifiability, while management accounting stresses relevance and promptness and may use reasonable estimates.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Cost accounting ascertains the cost per unit, job or process, so as to help in cost control and in fixing prices.
2. Financial accounting determines the overall profit or loss and the financial position of the enterprise as a whole, mainly for users outside the management.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: cost accounting ascertains cost per unit, job or process for control and pricing, while financial accounting gives overall profit or loss and position, mainly for outsiders.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Cost accounting is the narrower discipline, centred on the ascertainment and control of the cost of products and processes.
2. Management accounting is confined to cost data alone and makes no use of financial or other data.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is correct: cost accounting is narrower, centred on cost ascertainment and control. Statement 2 is wrong as management accounting also uses financial and other data.

q: Overhead, in cost accounting, is the aggregate of:

options.A: Direct material, direct labour and direct expenses
options.B: Indirect material, indirect labour and indirect expenses
options.C: Prime cost and direct expenses
options.D: Factory overheads and the profit of the period

e: Overhead is the aggregate of all indirect costs: indirect material plus indirect labour plus indirect expenses, which cannot be traced directly to a cost unit.

q: A costing clerk in a workshop finds that lubricating oil, cotton waste and small tools are consumed for the machines in general and cannot be traced to any particular job. In the elements of cost, these items are classified as:

options.A: Direct material of the jobs done on the machines
options.B: Direct expenses of the jobs
options.C: Administration overheads of the workshop
options.D: Indirect material, forming part of the factory overheads

e: Lubricating oil, cotton waste and small tools used for machines generally cannot be traced to a particular job, so they are indirect material forming part of factory overheads.

q: Fees paid for special designs and drawings got prepared exclusively for executing one particular customer's job are treated in the cost of that job as:

options.A: A part of the factory overheads
options.B: A part of the administration overheads
options.C: A direct (chargeable) expense of the job
options.D: A part of the selling overheads

e: Fees for designs and drawings prepared exclusively for one customer's job are directly chargeable to that job, so they are a direct expense of the job.

q: The wages of factory timekeepers and storekeepers, who serve the factory as a whole and are not employed on any single job, are classified in cost accounts as:

options.A: Indirect labour
options.B: Direct labour
options.C: Direct material
options.D: Direct expenses

e: Timekeepers and storekeepers serve the factory as a whole and not any single job, so their wages are indirect labour.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Advertisement and sales-promotion expenses incurred to secure orders are selling overheads.
2. The rent of a warehouse used only for storing finished goods awaiting despatch is a distribution overhead.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: advertisement and sales promotion to secure orders are selling overheads, and rent of a warehouse storing only finished goods awaiting despatch is a distribution overhead.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Grouping costs into factory, administration, selling and distribution costs is a classification of costs according to function.
2. Grouping costs into fixed, variable and semi-variable costs is a classification of costs according to behaviour (variability with output).
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: Neither 1 nor 2
options.B: 1 only
options.C: 2 only
options.D: Both 1 and 2

e: Both hold: factory, administration, selling and distribution is classification by function, while fixed, variable and semi-variable is classification by behaviour with output.

q: In a cost sheet, the cost of sales (total cost) of the goods sold is arrived at by:

options.A: Adding the selling and distribution overheads to the cost of goods sold
options.B: Adding the factory overheads to the cost of production
options.C: Deducting the selling overheads from the prime cost
options.D: Adding the profit to the works cost

e: Cost of sales is cost of goods sold plus selling and distribution overheads; this adds the cost of selling and delivering to the cost of the goods sold.

q: The direct material consumed in a factory is Rs 70,000, the direct labour is Rs 50,000 and the factory overheads are Rs 30,000. The conversion cost is:
e: Conversion cost = direct labour + factory overheads = Rs 50,000 + Rs 30,000 = Rs 80,000. Direct material is excluded as it is not a conversion cost.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Prime cost includes the direct material cost, but conversion cost does not.
2. Conversion cost includes the factory overheads, but prime cost does not.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: prime cost includes direct material but conversion cost does not, and conversion cost includes factory overheads but prime cost does not.

q: Whether a particular cost is a direct cost or an indirect cost depends on:

options.A: The amount of the cost incurred
options.B: The cost object — the job, unit or centre — chosen for tracing it; a cost that is direct to a department may be indirect to a unit of output produced in that department
options.C: Whether the cost is fixed or variable in nature
options.D: The month of the year in which the cost is incurred

e: Direct or indirect depends on the cost object chosen for tracing: a cost direct to a department may be indirect to a unit of output produced in that department.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The cost of materials still held in stock at the end of a period is an unexpired cost and is shown as an asset.
2. The cost of goods already sold continues to be shown as an asset until the sale proceeds are received in cash.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 is correct: material still in stock is an unexpired cost shown as an asset. Statement 2 is wrong as cost of goods sold is an expired cost, not an asset.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a book cost from an imputed (notional) cost?

options.A: A book cost involves an immediate cash payment, while an imputed cost does not involve any payment at all
options.B: A book cost is charged only in the financial accounts, while an imputed cost is charged only in the cost accounts
options.C: Both are hypothetical charges and neither of them appears in the books of account
options.D: A book cost, such as depreciation, is recorded in the books though it involves no current cash outlay, while an imputed cost is a hypothetical charge, such as interest on own capital, which is not recorded in the financial books

e: A book cost like depreciation is recorded in the books though no current cash is paid, while an imputed cost like interest on own capital is a hypothetical charge not recorded in financial books.

q: A proprietor works full-time as the manager of his own firm but draws no salary for his services. For a fair comparison of the firm's costs with those of a similar concern employing a paid manager, the cost accounts may take into account:

options.A: The salary actually drawn by the proprietor, which is nil
options.B: A notional (imputed) salary for the services rendered by the proprietor
options.C: The dividend payable on the capital of the firm
options.D: The income tax paid by the proprietor

e: For fair comparison, a notional or imputed salary for the proprietor-manager's services should be taken into account, even though he actually draws nil.

q:
Consider the following statements. For a cost to be relevant to a managerial decision, it must be:
1. A future cost, that is, a cost yet to be incurred and not one already incurred in the past.
2. A cost that differs between the alternative courses of action under consideration.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both conditions are needed: a relevant cost must be a future cost yet to be incurred, and it must differ between the alternatives under consideration.

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes differential cost from marginal cost?

options.A: Differential cost is the difference in total cost between two alternative courses of action (or levels of activity), while marginal cost is the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit
options.B: Differential cost relates to one additional unit only, while marginal cost relates to a change in the level of activity as a whole
options.C: Differential cost is a past cost, while marginal cost is a future cost
options.D: There is no difference between the two; the terms mean the same thing

e: Differential cost is the difference in total cost between two alternatives or levels of activity, while marginal cost is the change in total cost from producing one additional unit.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The expenditure on a staff-training programme, which management may postpone for a year without affecting current operations, is a committed fixed cost.
2. Depreciation on plant already purchased and rent payable under a long lease already signed are committed fixed costs, which cannot be avoided in the short run.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 2 only: depreciation on plant already bought and rent under a signed long lease are committed fixed costs. Staff training that can be postponed is discretionary, not committed.

q: A salesman is paid a fixed salary every month together with a commission calculated as a percentage of the sales made by him. His total remuneration is an example of a:

options.A: Purely fixed cost
options.B: Purely variable cost
options.C: Semi-variable (mixed) cost
options.D: Step cost

e: Fixed monthly salary is the fixed element and commission on sales is the variable element, so total remuneration is a semi-variable or mixed cost.

q: A firm requires one delivery van, with its driver, for despatching up to 500 parcels a day. As soon as the daily despatches rise beyond that level, a second van with its driver has to be engaged at once. The cost of the despatch vans behaves as a:

options.A: Step cost
options.B: Variable cost
options.C: Sunk cost
options.D: Imputed cost

e: Van and driver cost stays constant up to 500 parcels and then jumps at once when a second van is engaged, which is the behaviour of a step cost.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Depreciation of the factory plant is a product cost, which is carried in the value of stock until the goods are sold.
2. Depreciation of the delivery vehicles used for despatching finished goods is a period cost, which is charged against the revenue of the period in which it is incurred.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

e: Both hold: factory plant depreciation is a product cost carried in stock until sale, while delivery vehicle depreciation is a period cost charged against the period's revenue.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The rent of the factory office situated inside the works is an administration overhead.
2. The salary of the head-office accounts staff engaged on the general administration of the enterprise is an administration overhead.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 2 only: head-office accounts staff salary is administration overhead. Factory office rent inside the works is a factory overhead, not administration overhead.

q: Selling overheads are incurred in creating and stimulating demand and in securing orders. Distribution overheads, in contrast, are incurred:

options.A: In manufacturing the product in the factory
options.B: In administering the general office of the enterprise
options.C: After the sale is effected, in making the packed finished goods available for despatch and in delivering them to the customers
options.D: In securing orders from prospective customers

e: Distribution overheads arise after the sale is effected, in making packed finished goods available for despatch and delivering them to customers.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The cost of the fuel consumed by a particular train service can be traced directly to that service.
2. The cost of maintaining a section of track used by both coaching and goods trains is a common cost, to be apportioned between the two streams of traffic on an equitable basis.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: fuel for a particular train service is directly traceable to it, while track maintenance for both coaching and goods trains is a common cost to be apportioned equitably.

q: Break-even analysis commonly assumes that production and sales during the period are equal. The assumption means that:

options.A: The stock of finished goods goes on rising throughout the period
options.B: There is no change in the stock of finished goods, so the result is not affected by the valuation of opening and closing stock
options.C: The fixed costs of the period are nil
options.D: The selling price changes with every change in the stock level

e: Equal production and sales means no change in finished goods stock, so the result is not affected by valuation of opening and closing stock.

q: For a firm selling several products, break-even analysis rests, among others, on the assumption that:

options.A: The sales mix of the products remains constant in the budgeted proportions
options.B: Only one of the products is actually sold during the period
options.C: Every product of the firm has the same P/V ratio
options.D: The fixed costs are divided equally among all the products

e: For several products, break-even analysis assumes the sales mix remains constant in the budgeted proportions; otherwise the composite P/V ratio would change.

q: A practical limitation of break-even analysis is that:

options.A: Its results cannot be presented in the form of a chart
options.B: It takes no account of the selling price of the product
options.C: It requires every cost to be separated into a fixed and a variable element, whereas many costs are semi-variable and such separation can only be approximate
options.D: It can be applied only to a service undertaking and not to a factory

e: Many costs are semi-variable and can be split into fixed and variable elements only approximately, which is a practical limitation of break-even analysis.

q: Break-even analysis is described as essentially static because:

options.A: It is prepared only from the accounts of the past year
options.B: It shows neither a profit nor a loss at any level of sales
options.C: It assumes that no fixed cost is incurred by the enterprise
options.D: It is built on a given set of prices, costs, efficiency and product mix for a period, and ceases to hold good when any of these conditions changes

e: It is static because it is built on a given set of prices, costs, efficiency and product mix for a period, and ceases to hold when any of these conditions changes.

q:
Consider the following statements, the selling price and the variable cost per unit remaining unchanged:
1. An increase in the total fixed costs raises the break-even point of the firm.
2. An increase in the total fixed costs also raises the P/V ratio of the firm.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only: higher fixed costs raise the break-even point. The P/V ratio depends on price and variable cost, not fixed costs, so statement 2 is wrong.

q: If the selling price per unit of a product is raised, while its variable cost per unit and the total fixed costs remain unchanged, the break-even point will:

options.A: Rise, because the sales value increases
options.B: Fall, because the contribution per unit increases
options.C: Remain exactly the same as before
options.D: Become equal to the total fixed costs

e: A higher selling price with unchanged variable cost raises contribution per unit, so fewer units are needed to cover fixed costs and the break-even point falls.

q: A large margin of safety in a business indicates that:

options.A: The absolute amount of its profit must necessarily be large
options.B: Its fixed costs are nil
options.C: Its sales can fall considerably before the business reaches the break-even level and begins to incur a loss
options.D: Its P/V ratio is 100 per cent

e: A large margin of safety means actual sales are well above break-even, so sales can fall considerably before the business begins to incur a loss.

q: The marginal cost equation, S − V = F + P, expresses that:

options.A: Sales minus fixed cost is equal to variable cost plus profit
options.B: Variable cost is equal to fixed cost plus profit
options.C: Sales plus variable cost is equal to fixed cost plus profit
options.D: Sales minus variable cost, that is, the contribution, is equal to fixed cost plus profit

e: S - V = contribution, and contribution must cover fixed cost plus profit, so S - V = F + P.

q: Under marginal costing, the work-in-progress of a factory, like its finished stock, is valued at:

options.A: Total cost, including the fixed production overheads
options.B: Marginal (variable) cost only
options.C: Prime cost plus a share of the administration overheads
options.D: Selling price less the estimated profit on sale

e: Under marginal costing, work-in-progress and finished stock are valued at marginal or variable cost only; fixed production overheads are treated as period costs.

q: Marginal costing cannot by itself serve as the basis of long-term pricing, because in the long run:

options.A: The variable cost per unit disappears altogether
options.B: The fixed costs of the enterprise become variable costs
options.C: The selling price must recover the total cost, including the fixed costs, if the enterprise is to survive and earn a return
options.D: The contribution of every product becomes equal to its profit

e: In the long run the selling price must recover total cost including fixed costs, otherwise the enterprise cannot survive and earn a return, so marginal cost alone cannot base long-term pricing.

q: A P/V ratio of 40 per cent for a product means that:

options.A: Every rupee of sales yields a contribution of 40 paise, available towards meeting the fixed costs and providing profit
options.B: The profit of the enterprise is 40 per cent of its sales
options.C: The fixed costs are 40 per cent of the total cost
options.D: Every rupee of sales yields a profit of 40 paise after meeting all costs

e: A P/V ratio of 40 percent means every rupee of sales gives 40 paise of contribution towards meeting fixed costs and providing profit, not 40 paise of profit itself.

q: In a profit-volume (P/V) chart, in which profit and loss are plotted against the level of sales:

options.A: The sales line and the total cost line intersect each other
options.B: The profit line starts from the origin of the chart
options.C: The loss at zero sales is equal to the variable costs of the period
options.D: The point at which the profit line crosses the sales (horizontal) axis is the break-even point

e: In a P/V chart the break-even point is where the profit line crosses the sales or horizontal axis, where profit is zero.

q: A mechanised cleaning plant for a coaching depot costs Rs 11,90,000 and is expected to give a net cash inflow of Rs 1,70,000 every year. Its payback period is:

options.A: 6 years
options.B: 7 years
options.C: 8 years
options.D: 10 years

e: Payback = cost / annual net cash inflow = Rs 11,90,000 / Rs 1,70,000 = 7 years.

q: A project costing Rs 5,40,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,40,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,80,000 in Year 2 and Rs 2,20,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 2.5 years
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 3.5 years

e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 Rs 1,40,000, Year 2 Rs 3,20,000, Year 3 Rs 5,40,000, which equals the cost of Rs 5,40,000, so payback is 3 years.

q: A project costing Rs 7,50,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 2,50,000 in Year 1, Rs 3,00,000 in Year 2 and Rs 2,50,000 in Year 3. Its payback period is:

options.A: 2.80 years
options.B: 2.50 years
options.C: 3.00 years
options.D: 2.20 years

e: Cumulative after Year 2 = Rs 2,50,000 + Rs 3,00,000 = Rs 5,50,000. Balance Rs 2,00,000 / Rs 2,50,000 = 0.80 year, so payback = 2.80 years.

q: A doubling proposal requires an initial outlay of Rs 11,00,000. The present value of its expected cash inflows is Rs 12,75,000. Its Net Present Value is:
e: NPV = present value of inflows - outlay = Rs 12,75,000 - Rs 11,00,000 = Rs 1,75,000.

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 6,00,000. It will give cash inflows of Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 2, for which the present value factors are 0.90 and 0.81 respectively. Its Net Present Value is:
The present value of a net cash inflow of Rs 90,000 at the end of each year for 5 years, when the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.791, is:
e: Present value = annual inflow x annuity factor = Rs 90,000 x 3.791 = Rs 3,41,190.

q: Rs 4,50,000 is receivable at the end of Year 3. The present value factor for Year 3 at 10% is 0.751. The present value of the amount is:
e: Present value = Rs 4,50,000 x 0.751 = Rs 3,37,950.

q: The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 13,20,000 and its initial investment is Rs 12,00,000. Its Profitability Index is:
e: Profitability Index = PV of inflows / initial investment = Rs 13,20,000 / Rs 12,00,000 = 1.10.

q: An investment of Rs 7,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation of Rs 84,000. Its Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR = average annual profit / initial investment x 100 = Rs 84,000 / Rs 7,00,000 x 100 = 12 percent.

q: An investment of Rs 10,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 2,00,000 at the end of its life. Its average annual profit after depreciation is Rs 96,000. Its Average Rate of Return on the average investment is:
e: Average investment = (Rs 10,00,000 + Rs 2,00,000) / 2 = Rs 6,00,000. ARR = Rs 96,000 / Rs 6,00,000 x 100 = 16 percent.

q: A line capacity work is estimated to cost Rs 4 crore and is expected to give annual net earnings of Rs 52 lakh. The anticipated rate of return on the cost is:
e: Rate of return = annual net earnings / cost x 100 = Rs 52 lakh / Rs 4 crore (Rs 400 lakh) x 100 = 13 percent.

q: A proposal is estimated to cost Rs 2.5 crore. Its expected gross earnings are Rs 68 lakh a year and its expected working expenses are Rs 48 lakh a year. The anticipated rate of return on the cost is:
e: Net earnings = Rs 68 lakh - Rs 48 lakh = Rs 20 lakh. Return = Rs 20 lakh / Rs 2.5 crore (Rs 250 lakh) x 100 = 8 percent.

q: The Net Present Value of a project is (+) Rs 24,000 at a discount rate of 10% and (-) Rs 36,000 at a discount rate of 16%. By interpolation, its Internal Rate of Return is approximately:

A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 1,80,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 85,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 95,000 at the end of Year 2 and Rs 1,10,000 at the end of Year 3. Its discounted payback period is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 2.5 years
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 1.5 years

e: Cumulative discounted inflows: Year 1 Rs 85,000, Year 2 Rs 85,000 + Rs 95,000 = Rs 1,80,000, equal to the outlay, so discounted payback is 2 years.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 2,80,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,10,000 at the end of Year 1, Rs 1,20,000 at the end of Year 2 and Rs 1,00,000 at the end of Year 3. Its discounted payback period is:

options.A: 2 years
options.B: 2.5 years
options.C: 3 years
options.D: 2.8 years

e: Cumulative after Year 2 = Rs 1,10,000 + Rs 1,20,000 = Rs 2,30,000. Balance Rs 50,000 / Rs 1,00,000 = 0.5 year, so discounted payback = 2.5 years.

q: A project costing Rs 5,60,000 has a present value of operating cash inflows of Rs 5,10,000 and a present value of salvage value of Rs 90,000. Its Net Present Value is:
e: NPV = PV of operating inflows + PV of salvage - cost = Rs 5,10,000 + Rs 90,000 - Rs 5,60,000 = Rs 40,000.

q: A project shows an annual accounting profit after depreciation of Rs 1,48,000. The depreciation charged in arriving at this profit is Rs 52,000. The annual net cash inflow from the project is:
e: Depreciation is non-cash, so annual net cash inflow = accounting profit + depreciation = Rs 1,48,000 + Rs 52,000 = Rs 2,00,000.

q: A proposed facility will bring additional earnings of Rs 3,20,000 a year and will involve additional cash working expenses of Rs 1,90,000 a year. The incremental net cash inflow per year is:
e: Incremental net cash inflow = additional earnings - additional cash working expenses = Rs 3,20,000 - Rs 1,90,000 = Rs 1,30,000.

q: A project costing Rs 4,20,000 will give a net cash inflow of Rs 1,40,000 at the end of each year for 4 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 4 years at 10% is 3.170. Its Net Present Value is:
The present value of the benefits expected from a project is Rs 27,00,000 and the present value of its costs is Rs 22,50,000. Its benefit-cost ratio is:
e: Benefit-cost ratio = PV of benefits / PV of costs = Rs 27,00,000 / Rs 22,50,000 = 1.20.

q: Residential quarters are built at a cost of Rs 80 lakh. The annual assessed rent recoverable for them is Rs 4,80,000. The yield by way of assessed rent on the cost is:
e: Yield = assessed rent / cost x 100 = Rs 4,80,000 / Rs 80,00,000 x 100 = 6 percent.

q: At a discount rate of 14%, the present value of the cash inflows of a project is Rs 6,72,000 and its initial cost is also Rs 6,72,000. The Internal Rate of Return of the project is:
e: At 14 percent the PV of inflows equals the initial cost, so NPV is zero at 14 percent, which by definition is the Internal Rate of Return.

q: A project requires plant costing Rs 9,25,000 and additional working capital of Rs 1,75,000 at the very start. The total initial cash outflow of the project is:
e: Total initial outflow = plant cost + working capital at start = Rs 9,25,000 + Rs 1,75,000 = Rs 11,00,000.

q: Two mutually exclusive proposals are under consideration and funds are available for either. The smaller proposal shows the higher Internal Rate of Return, while the larger proposal shows the higher Net Present Value. The proposal to be preferred is:

options.A: The one with the higher Internal Rate of Return, in every case
options.B: The smaller proposal, because its outlay is less
options.C: The one with the shorter payback period
options.D: The one with the higher Net Present Value, as it adds more in absolute present value terms

e: For mutually exclusive proposals, the one with higher NPV is preferred because it adds more in absolute present value terms, even if the other has a higher IRR.

q: A project may show more than one Internal Rate of Return when:

options.A: Its net cash flows change sign more than once during its life, for example because of a large renewal outflow in a middle year
options.B: Its life exceeds ten years
options.C: Its initial cost is very large
options.D: Its annual cash inflows are uniform

e: More than one IRR can arise when net cash flows change sign more than once during the project's life, for example due to a large renewal outflow in a middle year.

q: Even the discounted payback period suffers from the limitation that it:

options.A: Ignores the time value of money
options.B: Cannot be worked out for uneven cash inflows
options.C: Ignores the cash inflows arising after the discounted payback period
options.D: Requires accounting profit instead of cash flows

e: Even discounted payback ignores all cash inflows arising after the discounted payback period, so later profitability is not considered.

q: The payback period is found useful in appraisal mainly as:

options.A: A complete measure of the profitability of a project
options.B: A rough screen for liquidity and risk, favouring proposals whose outlay is recovered early
options.C: A substitute for the Discounted Cash Flow technique
options.D: A method which values every future inflow at its present value

e: Payback is mainly a rough screen for liquidity and risk, favouring proposals whose outlay is recovered early; it is not a complete measure of profitability.

q: In Discounted Cash Flow appraisal, depreciation charged on the project assets is treated as:

options.A: A cash outflow of the year in which it is charged
options.B: An addition to the initial cost of the project
options.C: A receipt of the final year of the project
options.D: Not itself a cash outflow; the accounting profit is adjusted by adding it back to arrive at the cash flow

e: Depreciation is not itself a cash outflow; accounting profit is adjusted by adding it back to arrive at the cash flow for DCF appraisal.

q: The estimated capital cost of a work rises, while its anticipated earnings remain unchanged. The anticipated rate of return of the work will:

options.A: Fall
options.B: Rise
options.C: Remain unchanged
options.D: Become equal to its payback period

e: Return = earnings / cost. With earnings unchanged and estimated capital cost higher, the denominator rises, so the anticipated rate of return falls.

q: Two proposals have the same total undiscounted cash inflows and the same initial cost. One receives its inflows earlier and the other receives them later. The proposal with the higher Net Present Value will be:

options.A: The one receiving its inflows later
options.B: Both, as their Net Present Values will be equal
options.C: The one receiving its inflows earlier
options.D: The one with the longer life

e: Earlier inflows are discounted less than later inflows, so with equal totals and cost, the proposal receiving inflows earlier has the higher NPV.

q: A project gives only a modest return on the receipts of the Railways themselves, but it saves considerable travelling time and reduces road congestion. These wider benefits are taken into account in:

options.A: The Financial Internal Rate of Return alone
options.B: The Economic Internal Rate of Return
options.C: The payback period
options.D: The depreciation charge of the project

e: Wider benefits like time saved and reduced road congestion, beyond the Railways' own receipts, are taken into account in the Economic Internal Rate of Return.

q: A new branch line is expected to feed additional traffic on to the existing main line, thereby increasing earnings on that line as well. This additional benefit is an example of:

options.A: A transfer payment
options.B: A sunk benefit
options.C: A salvage value
options.D: A network effect

e: Extra traffic fed onto the existing main line by a new branch line, raising earnings on that line too, is a network effect.

q: In the economic appraisal of a project, a cash subsidy received for the project is treated as:

options.A: A transfer payment, and is not counted as an economic benefit
options.B: A net addition to the national income
options.C: A reduction in the initial cost of the project
options.D: A sunk receipt

e: In economic appraisal a cash subsidy is a transfer payment: it transfers purchasing power without adding to national income, so it is not counted as an economic benefit.

q: A number of independent projects are under appraisal and there is no shortage of funds. The projects to be accepted are:

options.A: Only the single project with the highest Net Present Value
options.B: Only the single project with the highest Internal Rate of Return
options.C: All the projects which show a positive Net Present Value
options.D: Only the project with the shortest payback period

e: With no shortage of funds and independent projects, all projects showing a positive NPV should be accepted, as each adds to value.

q: The Profitability Index of a project is less than 1. It follows that:

options.A: Its Net Present Value is positive
options.B: Its Net Present Value is negative, as the present value of its inflows is less than its outlay
options.C: Its Net Present Value is exactly zero
options.D: Its payback period is less than one year

e: Profitability Index below 1 means PV of inflows is less than the outlay, so NPV = PV of inflows - outlay must be negative.

q: The Internal Rate of Return of a project works out below the required rate of return used for judging it. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Accept it, because some return is still earned
options.B: Accept it, because its Net Present Value must be positive
options.C: Ignore the Internal Rate of Return altogether
options.D: Reject it, as its Net Present Value at the required rate would be negative

e: IRR below the required rate means NPV at the required rate would be negative, so the project should be rejected.

q: A weakness of the Average Rate of Return method is that:

options.A: It may change if a different method of depreciation is adopted, even though the cash flows of the project remain the same
options.B: It is based entirely on cash flows
options.C: It discounts the future profits of the project
options.D: It is not affected by the accounting profit at all

e: ARR uses accounting profit, so a different depreciation method changes the profit and the ARR even though the project's cash flows remain the same.

q: Which of the following statements about the payback period is correct?

options.A: The project with the shortest payback period always has the highest Net Present Value
options.B: The payback period is a direct measure of the profitability of a project
options.C: A project with the shortest payback period need not be the most profitable over its full life
options.D: The payback period takes into account every cash inflow of the project

e: Shortest payback need not mean most profitable over the full life, because payback ignores inflows after the payback period and overall profitability.

q: Rs 3,50,000 has already been spent on a geological survey for a proposed line. While deciding now whether to take up the line, this amount should be:

options.A: Added to the cost of the project
options.B: Treated as a sunk cost and ignored; only the future costs and benefits should be considered
options.C: Recovered from the earnings of the first year
options.D: Added to the cost together with interest on it

e: Rs 3,50,000 already spent on the survey is a sunk cost; the decision now should consider only future costs and benefits, so it is ignored.

q: A project is to be housed in a railway building which could otherwise be leased out for rent. In appraising the project, the rent forgone is to be treated as:

options.A: A sunk cost
options.B: No cost at all, as no cash is paid out
options.C: A cash receipt of the project
options.D: An opportunity cost of the project

e: Rent forgone by using a building that could otherwise be leased out is an opportunity cost of the project and must be counted in appraisal.

q: In the appraisal of a workshop project, the residual value expected to be realised from its plant at the end of the appraisal period is treated as:

options.A: A cash inflow of the final year
options.B: A cash outflow of the first year
options.C: An addition to the initial cost
options.D: A working expense of every year

e: Residual value of plant expected at the end of the appraisal period is realised then, so it is treated as a cash inflow of the final year.

q: In the test of remunerativeness of a railway work, the anticipated annual net earnings are expressed as a percentage of:

options.A: The average annual working expenses
options.B: The total gross earnings of the railway
options.C: The initial estimated cost of the work
options.D: The salvage value of the work

e: In the test of remunerativeness, anticipated annual net earnings are expressed as a percentage of the initial estimated cost of the work.

q: Works undertaken to meet a safety requirement are generally:

options.A: Required to earn the highest rate of return among all works
options.B: Exempt from the requirement of financial justification
options.C: Taken up only as Public-Private Partnership projects
options.D: Charged to the Depreciation Reserve Fund in every case

e: Works undertaken to meet a safety requirement are generally exempt from the requirement of financial justification, as safety is not judged by return alone.

q: A complete financial appraisal of a proposal must take into account:

options.A: Only the initial capital cost of the work
options.B: Only the earnings expected in the first year
options.C: Only the salvage value at the end of the work
options.D: The initial capital cost as well as the recurring maintenance and working expenses

e: A complete appraisal must take into account both the initial capital cost and the recurring maintenance and working expenses, not any one item alone.

q: If the discount rate used in appraisal is increased, the present value of a given cash inflow expected in a future year will:

options.A: Decrease
options.B: Increase
options.C: Remain unchanged
options.D: Become equal to the future amount

e: A higher discount rate gives a smaller present value factor, so the present value of a given future cash inflow decreases.

q: A zonal railway earned gross traffic receipts of Rs 1,60,000 crore during a year, while its gross working expenses for the year were Rs 1,36,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio for the year is:
e: Operating Ratio = gross working expenses / gross traffic receipts x 100 = Rs 1,36,000 / Rs 1,60,000 x 100 = 85 percent.

q: The Operating Ratio of a railway is 92% and its gross traffic receipts for the year are Rs 2,25,000 crore. Its gross working expenses for the year are:

options.A: Rs 2,44,565 crore
options.B: Rs 2,07,000 crore
options.C: Rs 2,25,000 crore
options.D: Rs 18,000 crore

e: Gross working expenses = Operating Ratio x receipts = 92 percent x Rs 2,25,000 crore = Rs 2,07,000 crore.

q: Zone A reports an Operating Ratio of 87% and Zone B an Operating Ratio of 93% for the same year. Judged by this indicator alone:

options.A: Zone A is the more efficient, as it retains Rs 13 out of every Rs 100 earned after meeting gross working expenses, against only Rs 7 retained by Zone B
options.B: Zone B is the more efficient, as a higher Operating Ratio always denotes better performance
options.C: The two zones are equally efficient, since both ratios are below 100%
options.D: No comparison is possible, because the Operating Ratio says nothing about expenses in relation to earnings

e: A lower Operating Ratio is better: Zone A retains Rs 13 per Rs 100 earned against Zone B's Rs 7, so Zone A is more efficient on this indicator alone.

q:
Consider the following statements about the Operating Ratio of Indian Railways:
1. It is worked out by expressing the gross working expenses, which include the appropriations to the Depreciation Reserve Fund and the Pension Fund, as a percentage of the gross earnings.
2. It is worked out by expressing the net earnings as a percentage of the capital-at-charge.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Statement 1 only: Operating Ratio is gross working expenses, including appropriations to DRF and Pension Fund, as a percentage of gross earnings. Statement 2 describes return on capital.

q: The gross earnings of a railway rose during a year, yet its Operating Ratio worsened (rose) in the same year. This can happen when:

options.A: Gross working expenses fall while earnings rise
options.B: Gross working expenses rise proportionately faster than the earnings
options.C: Capital expenditure during the year rises sharply
options.D: The capital-at-charge of the railway increases

e: Operating Ratio worsens despite higher earnings when gross working expenses rise proportionately faster than the earnings, increasing the expenses-to-earnings percentage.

q: A railway's gross working expenses for a year are Rs 2,10,000 crore against gross traffic receipts of Rs 2,00,000 crore. Its Operating Ratio is:
e: Operating Ratio = Rs 2,10,000 / Rs 2,00,000 x 100 = 105 percent, meaning working expenses exceed receipts.

q: A divisional officer suggests that the Operating Ratio of his zone can be improved directly by booking a large programme of new-line construction during the year. The suggestion is not sound, because:

options.A: New-line construction is never charged to capital
options.B: The Operating Ratio is computed only for divisions and not for zones
options.C: Capital expenditure on new lines is not a part of the gross working expenses that form the numerator of the Operating Ratio, so such spending does not by itself improve the ratio
options.D: Gross earnings cease to count in the Operating Ratio once a new line is opened

e: New-line construction is capital expenditure, not part of gross working expenses forming the numerator of the Operating Ratio, so it does not by itself improve the ratio.

q: A recognised limitation of using the Operating Ratio alone for comparing the efficiency of different zonal railways is that:

options.A: It cannot be computed from the published accounts of a zone
options.B: The zones differ in their traffic mix, average lead of traffic, terrain and the proportion of unremunerative services they are obliged to run, so identical ratios need not mean identical managerial efficiency
options.C: It takes into account the capital employed by each zone
options.D: It is expressed in money terms rather than as a percentage

e: Zones differ in traffic mix, average lead, terrain and proportion of unremunerative services, so identical Operating Ratios need not mean identical managerial efficiency.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Operating Ratio measures how much of the earnings is absorbed by working expenses, but it takes no account of the capital employed in producing those earnings.
2. Judging a railway's financial performance by the Operating Ratio together with the Return on Capital gives a fuller picture than the Operating Ratio alone.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

e: Both hold: Operating Ratio ignores capital employed, so judging performance by Operating Ratio together with Return on Capital gives a fuller picture.

q: A railway with an Operating Ratio of 84% spends, on gross working expenses, out of every Rs 100 of gross earnings:

options.A: Rs 84, leaving Rs 16 of the earnings after meeting the gross working expenses
options.B: Rs 16, leaving Rs 84 after meeting the gross working expenses
options.C: Rs 84 on capital works alone
options.D: Rs 100, the balance of Rs 16 being met from borrowings

e: An Operating Ratio of 84 percent means Rs 84 out of every Rs 100 of gross earnings is spent on gross working expenses, leaving Rs 16 after meeting them.
